Objective over Architecture: Fraud Detection
Under Extreme Imbalance in Bank Account
Opening Wenxi Sun 1,† , Qiannan Shen 2,† , Yijun Gao 3 , Qinkai Mao 4 , Tongsong Qi 5 and Shuo Xu 6, ∗

These authors contributed equally to this work. Abstract: Fraud in nancial services—especially account opening fraud—poses major 1 operational and reputational risks. Static rules struggle to adapt to evolving tactics, miss- 2 ing novel patterns and generating excessive false positives. Machine learning promises 3 adaptive detection, but deployment faces severe class imbalance: in the NeurIPS 2022 4 BAF Base benchmark used here, fraud prevalence is 1.10%. Standard metrics (accuracy, 5
f1_weighted ) can look strong while doing little for the minority class. We compare logistic 6 regression, SVM (RBF), Random Forest, LightGBM, and a GRU model on N = 1 , 000 , 000 7 accounts under a unied preprocessing pipeline. All models are trained to minimize their 8 loss function, while congurations are selected on a stratied development set using valida- 9 tion f1_weighted . For the four classical models, class weighting in the loss ( class_weight 10
∈ { None , ‘balanced’ } ) is treated as a hyperparameter and tuned. Similarly, the GRU is 11 trained with a xed class-weighted cross-entropy loss that up-weights fraud cases. This 12 ensures that both model families leverage weighted training objectives, while their nal 13 hyperparameters are consistently selected by the f1_weighted metric. Despite similar 14 AUCs and aligned feature importance across families, the classical models converge to 15 high-precision, low-recall solutions (1-6% fraud recall), whereas the GRU recovers 78% 16 recall at 5% precision (AUC = 0.8800). Under extreme imbalance, objective choice and 17
operating point matter at least as much as architecture. 18 Keywords: fraud detection; bank account opening fraud; imbalanced classication; 19
precision-recall trade-off; gated recurrent unit 20 1. Introduction 21 Fraud in the nancial services sector is a persistent and evolving threat, extending far 22 beyond transaction-level scams. A particularly costly and growing danger is bank account 23 opening fraud , where criminals use stolen or synthetic identities to establish new accounts 24 [ 1 ]. These accounts then serve as conduits for money laundering, unauthorized credit access, 25 and other nancial crimes, costing institutions billions annually and posing signicant 26 operational and reputational risks [ 2 ]. These challenges are not unique to banking; the 27
2 of 17 insurance industry faces analogous problems in claims fraud and identity-related schemes, 28
which present the same data-driven challenges [ 3 – 5 ]. 29 Historically, the rst line of defense was traditional detection frameworks built on 30 static, hard-coded rules (e.g., agging mismatched addresses). The core challenge of these 31 systems is their rigidity. As fraud tactics evolve, these static rules fail to adapt, leading to 32 a dual failure: they miss novel fraudulent patterns while simultaneously overwhelming 33 investigators with a high volume of false positives. The velocity of modern digital nance 34 renders these manual or static systems infeasible, creating an urgent need for automated, 35
adaptive solutions [ 6 ]. 36 To overcome these limitations, machine learning (ML) has been widely adopted for its 37 ability to learn subtle, complex patterns from heterogeneous data [ 7 ]. These models are now 38 critical components of modern FinTech platforms, often deployed on cloud infrastructure 39 to provide the low-latency predictions essential for real-time decisions. However, applying 40 ML in this domain introduces its own formidable challenge: severe class imbalance [ 8 ]. 41 In the dataset for this study, fraudulent applications constitute only 1.10% of all cases. 42 This imbalance creates a paradox: models trained to optimize standard metrics (like 43 accuracy or weighted-F1) are incentivized to predict the majority (non-fraud) class, creating 44 a misleading illusion of performance while failing to detect the very events they were built 45
to nd [ 9 ]. 46 The application of machine learning to nancial fraud is well-documented, with ex- 47 tensive surveys highlighting the persistent challenge of class imbalance and rare event 48 detection [ 10 , 11 ]. These comprehensive reviews emphasize a critical pitfall in fraud analyt- 49 ics: the reliance on accuracy-focused evaluation metrics, which can mask poor performance 50 on the minority class. To combat this, the literature has proposed various remediation 51 strategies, ranging from data-level techniques to algorithm-level approaches such as cost- 52 sensitive learning and anomaly detection [ 12 ]. However, while these individual methods 53 are well-established, there is often ambiguity regarding the comparative impact of the 54 model architecture versus the optimization objective in extremely imbalanced settings ( < 1% 55 prevalence). This study builds upon this literature by isolating these factors; rather than 56 proposing a novel complex architecture, we provide a controlled evaluation demonstrating 57
that the choice of objective function outweighs the choice of model family. 58 This paper provides a rigorous empirical comparison of classical and deep learning 59 approaches on a large-scale, public benchmark for bank account fraud detection [ 13 ]. We 60 systematically evaluate a suite of models: Logistic Regression (LR) [ 14 ], Support Vector 61 Machine (SVM) [ 15 ], Random Forest (RF) [ 16 ], LightGBM (LGBM) [ 17 ], and a custom 62 Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) network [ 18 ]. We specically investigate how these models 63 behave under a common hyperparameter-tuning rule while retaining the default training 64 objectives of their respective Python implementations. Concretely, all models share the 65 same preprocessing pipeline and are tuned on a stratied development set using the 66 validation weighted F1-score ( f1_weighted ) as the selection metric, while each model 67 optimises the default loss provided by its underlying Python function, with class weighting 68
enabled when selected during hyperparameter search. 69 Our results demonstrate two key ndings. First, we conrm that all classical models 70 optimized for standard metrics show limited efcacy, identifying almost no fraudulent 71 cases (1-6% recall). Second, we show that the GRU model, trained with a class-weighted 72 loss function, successfully overcomes this challenge, identifying 78% of all fraud. However, 73 this success exposes the central, practical challenge of this domain: a severe precision- 74 recall trade-off [ 19 ]. The high recall is achieved at the cost of extremely low precision (5%), 75
creating a signicant operational burden of false positives. 76
3 of 17 1.1. Motivation and Research Questions 77 We frame the study around three research questions (RQs) that the industry faces 78
under extreme imbalance: 79
1. RQ1: How do classical models (LR, SVM, RF, LGBM) behave when tuned and selected 80 using f1_weighted on a 1.10% prevalence dataset, and what failure modes emerge for 81
the minority class? 82
2. RQ2: To what extent can a class-weighted objective (here, with a GRU) recover 83 minority-class recall, and what precision (false-positive workload) trade-offs does this 84
entail? 85
3. RQ3: Do model families converge on the same high-signal features, implying that 86
objective choice—not signal scarcity—drives minority-class performance gaps? 87
1.2. Contributions 88
This paper makes four contributions aligned with those questions: 89
• A controlled, apples-to-apples comparison on the 1M-example BAF “Base” benchmark 90 with a unied preprocessing pipeline across classical models and a GRU architecture. 91
• An explicit demonstration of the objective-induced failure: using f1_weighted as the 92 selection criterion yields negligible fraud recall despite apparently strong aggregate 93
scores. 94
• Evidence that class-weighted training substantially increases recall (to 78%) while 95 quantifying the implied review burden (low precision); we report simple workload 96
proxies (e.g., FPs per TP) alongside standard metrics. 97
• A cross-family feature importance concordance showing that all models surface 98 the same core signals (e.g., name_email_similarity , velocity_24h ), supporting the 99
claim that objective choice—not feature discovery—explains the gap. 100
1.3. Terminology and Evaluation Framing 101 Throughout, we use operational cost to denote the human-review workload implied by 102 false positives at the chosen operating threshold. While ROC-AUC remains informative 103 for ranking, under 1.10% prevalence we emphasize precision–recall behavior and report 104
weighted-F1 only to reect legacy selection practices that can mislead in this setting. 105
1.4. Scope and Limitations 106 The focus is account opening fraud on the BAF synthetic benchmark; we do not model 107 post-opening transactional streams, cost-sensitive training beyond class weighting, or 108 production controls (e.g., case management, feedback loops). As the dataset is synthetic, 109 external validity may vary by institution and geography; nevertheless, the imbalance- 110 driven phenomena we document are generic to credit, banking, and insurance onboarding 111
contexts. 112 Finally, through a comparative feature importance analysis, we show that all models— 113 both the failing classical ones and the successful GRU—demonstrate a high degree of con- 114 sensus on the most predictive features, such as name_email_similarity and velocity_24h . 115 This provides the critical insight that the failure of the classical models was not one of 116 feature identication, but one of objective. This paper’s contribution is a rigorous analysis 117 of this trade-off, demonstrating how, in an imbalanced domain, the problem shifts from 118
one of detection (recall) to one of operational cost (precision). 119 The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 details the dataset, 120 preprocessing pipeline, and model architectures. Section 3 presents the comparative per- 121 formance and feature importance analysis. Section 4 discusses the implications of these 122
ndings. 123
4 of 17 2. Methods 124 This section presents the methodological framework developed to systematically 125 evaluate the effectiveness of classical and deep learning models for a highly imbalanced 126 nancial fraud detection task [ 6 ]. We begin by describing the dataset and the robust pre- 127 processing pipeline constructed to handle mixed numerical and categorical data types. 128 Next, we outline the architectures and optimization procedures for traditional machine 129 learning (LR, SVM, RF, LGBM) and an advanced recurrent neural model (GRU), including 130 the specic hyperparameter tuning strategies employed. We then dene the quantitative 131 evaluation metrics, with a focus on statistical validation via bootstrapping, which is essen- 132 tial for imbalanced classication. Finally, we detail the model-specic and model-agnostic 133 techniques used to compute and compare feature importance, a critical step for model 134
interpretability. 135
2.1. Data Preprocessing and Preparation 136 This study utilizes the Bank Account Fraud (BAF) dataset, a large-scale, privacy- 137 preserving benchmark for tabular fraud detection released at NeurIPS 2022 [ 13 ]. We use 138 the "Base" variant, which contains approximately one million ( N = 1,000,000) synthetic 139 bank account applications generated from a real-world, anonymized source. Each record 140 is described by a range of features and includes a binary label, fraud_bool (1: fraud, 0: 141
non-fraud), to indicate if the application was fraudulent. 142 It is important to clarify the provenance of this data. The BAF dataset is synthetic, 143 generated using a tabular Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) trained on real-world 144 transaction data to preserve privacy while maintaining statistical delity. As a synthetic 145 dataset, it avoids the privacy constraints of real banking data but relies on the assumption 146 that the GAN successfully captured the complex interactions of real-world fraud. It speci- 147 cally models "synthetic identity fraud," where criminals combine real (e.g., social security 148
numbers) and fake (e.g., names/emails) information to create a new, ctitious identity. 149 A dening characteristic of this dataset is its severe class imbalance. Fraudulent 150 applications constitute only 1.10% of the total records (11,029 fraud instances vs. 988,971 151 non-fraud instances). This severe imbalance is the central methodological challenge that 152
informs our strategies for model training, hyperparameter tuning, and evaluation [ 20 ]. 153 To ensure consistent and reproducible feature engineering, a comprehensive prepro- 154 cessing pipeline was constructed using scikit-learn ’s ColumnTransformer [ 21 ]. The raw 155 dataset contains 32 columns. After excluding the target label ( fraud_bool ), 31 potential 156 features remain. From these, we explicitly removed two uninformative columns, source 157 and month , resulting in exactly 29 input features used for modeling. These comprised 158 16 numerical features (e.g., income , velocity_6h , customer_age ) and 13 categorical fea- 159 tures (e.g., payment_type , employment_status , device_os ). The pipeline applied distinct 160
transformations to each data type: 161
1. Numerical Feature Pipeline: Numerical features were processed with a two-step 162 sequence. First, missing values were imputed using the median value of the respective 163 column. Second, all numerical features were standardized using StandardScaler , 164
transforming them to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. 165
2. Categorical Feature Pipeline: Categorical features were similarly processed. First, 166 missing values were imputed with a constant string placeholder ( "__missing__" ). 167 Second, the features were transformed using OneHotEncoder , which creates a sparse 168
binary vector for each unique category. 169 This preprocessor object was t only on the training data and subsequently used to 170 transform all data splits, thereby preventing any information leakage from the validation 171
or test sets. 172
5 of 17 The original training data, X_train , consisted of 800,000 records and 31 features. For 173 the deep learning approach (GRU), the 29 selected raw features were used directly as 174 an input sequence ( T = 29). For the classical models, after applying the preprocessor , 175 which uses 16 numerical features and 13 categorical features, the categorical variables 176 were expanded, meaning the nal, transformed data matrix had 59 features. This resulted 177 from the 16 numerical features being scaled and the 13 categorical features being one-hot 178 encoded into 43 distinct columns. The nal test set was similarly transformed from (200000, 179
31) to (200000, 59). 180
2.2. Experimental Setup 181 To facilitate rigorous model development and evaluation, the dataset was partitioned 182
into several distinct sets: 183
1. Training and Test Split: The full dataset ( N = 1,000,000) was divided into a primary 184 training set (80%, or 800,000 records) and a nal, held-out test set (20%, or 200,000 185 records). This split was stratied by the fraud_bool label to ensure the 1.10% positive 186
class ratio was precisely maintained in both partitions. 187
2. Hyperparameter Tuning Set: As grid-searching on 800,000 records is computationally 188 prohibitive, a smaller development set ( N = 10,000) was created by sub-sampling from 189 the training set, again using stratication. This smaller, balanced set was used for the 190
GridSearchCV process for all classical machine learning models. 191
3. Deep Learning Split: For the GRU model, the 800,000-record training set was further 192 subdivided into a new training partition (80%, or 640,000 records) and a validation 193 partition (20%, or 160,000 records). This split was used for the randomized hyperpa- 194
rameter search and for early stopping during model training. 195
Reproducibility and Environment 196 All experiments were executed in Google Colab using the standard CPU/GPU run- 197 times available at the time of study. Because Colab environments are ephemeral and 198 hardware/library versions may vary across sessions, we xed global random seeds across 199 Python/ numpy / scikit-learn / PyTorch and kept all preprocessing t strictly on the train- 200 ing split. Hyperparameter searches were bounded by a per–model-family wall-clock budget 201 with graceful early termination, returning the incumbent best conguration. These prac- 202 tices allow re-runs in Colab to match our reported performance within expected stochastic 203
variation, without relying on a xed machine image. 204
2.3. Model Architectures 205 We implemented and evaluated a suite of four classical machine learning models 206 and one deep learning model, each selected to represent a different class of algorithmic 207
approach to this classication problem. 208

2.3.2. Deep Learning Model: Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) Model 254 To capture complex, non-linear feature interactions, we designed a custom deep 255 learning model ( GRUSentimentModel ) that treats the tabular data as an ordered sequence. 256 The core of this model is the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) [ 18 ], an advanced recurrent 257

3. Imbalance Handling: This was the primary focus of training. 294
• For classical models, the class_weight=’balanced’ parameter was included in 295 the grid search, which automatically adjusts weights inversely proportional to 296
class frequencies. 297
• For the GRU model, this was implemented by calculating class weights on 298 the training set and passing them to the nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=...) 299 function. This penalizes misclassications of the minority (fraud) class more 300
heavily. 301 To facilitate complete reproduction of these results and allow other researchers to build 302 upon this work, the full source code—including the preprocessing pipeline, class-weight 303 implementation, and model training scripts—are available at rst author GitHub (the link 304
will be provided upon acceptance). 305
2.5. Evaluation Metrics 306 Given the severe class imbalance, accuracy is a misleading metric [ 20 ]. Our evaluation 307 focused on a suite of metrics that provide a nuanced view of model performance on both 308 the minority and majority classes [ 19 ]. For a binary classication problem, we dene True 309
Positives (TP), False Positives (FP), and False Negatives (FN). 310
Precision =
TP TP + FP
9 of 17 Precision measures the proportion of positive (fraud) predictions that were correct. High 311
precision is critical to minimize operational costs from false alarms. 312
Recall =
TP TP + FN Recall (or True Positive Rate) measures the proportion of actual fraud cases that the model 313 successfully identied. High recall is critical for minimizing risk and preventing fraudulent 314
transactions. 315
F1 = 2 ·
Precision · Recall Precision + Recall The F1-score is the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, providing a single score that 316 balances this trade-off [ 19 ]. We report the weighted F1-score as a primary metric, which 317
accounts for the class imbalance. 318 For all point-estimate metrics (Precision, Recall, F1), we utilize the standard classi- 319 cation threshold of τ = 0.5. While we acknowledge that operational thresholds in fraud 320 detection are typically tuned to specic cost constraints (as discussed in Section 4), utilizing 321 a xed, neutral threshold of 0.5 allows for a consistent, "ceteris paribus" comparison of the 322
intrinsic probability distributions generated by the different architectures. 323 Furthermore, we assess the model’s ability to distinguish between classes using the 324 Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve and its corresponding Area Under the 325
Curve (AUC). 326
TPR =
TP TP + FN
, FPR =
FP FP + TN The AUC represents the probability that the model will rank a randomly chosen positive 327
sample higher than a randomly chosen negative sample. 328 To assess the stability of our point-estimate metrics, we implemented a bootstrapping 329 procedure ( N = 1000 iterations) to compute the 95% Condence Intervals (CI) for both 330
the weighted F1-Score and the AUC on the test set. 331
2.6. Feature Importance Analysis 332 To ensure model interpretability and understand the key drivers of fraud, we em- 333
ployed a combination of model-specic and model-agnostic techniques. 334
1. Coefcient-Based (LR): For the Logistic Regression model, the absolute values of 335 the tted coef_ corresponding to each feature were used as a direct measure of 336
importance. 337
2. Tree-Based (RF, LGBM): For the ensemble tree models, the native feature_importances_ 338 attribute was used. This score is typically based on Gini impurity reduction (RF) or 339
gain (LGBM) aggregated across all trees in the ensemble. 340
3. Permutation Importance (SVM, GRU): For the non-linear ’rbf’ SVM and the "black- 341 box" GRU model, we used permutation feature importance . This model-agnostic 342 technique measures the decrease in the model’s F1-score when the values of a single 343 feature are randomly shufed. This procedure was executed for 6 − 10 repeats on 344 a 3,000-record subsample for computational efciency. For the GRU, this was per- 345 formed on the original features (e.g., income ) before the embedding stage to maintain 346
interpretability. 347
3. Results 348 This section presents the empirical results of the machine learning and deep learn- 349 ing models, evaluated on the held-out test set ( N = 200,000). The analysis is pre- 350 sented in two parts. First, we examine the performance of the classical models as op- 351
10 of 17 timized by the GridSearchCV process, which used f1_weighted as its primary scoring 352 metric. Second, we analyze the performance of models specically re-trained using the 353
class_weight=’balanced’ technique to address the severe class imbalance. 354
3.1. Hyperparameter Optimization and Tuning Cost 355 Table 1 summarizes the best settings identied by cross-validated search (see Methods) 356 and the wall-clock time required to complete tuning for each model. The classical baselines 357 converged quickly (5.4–46.6s): the SVM favored an RBF kernel with C = 10 and γ = scale , 358 while logistic regression selected L
2 regularization with the lbfgs solver. For tree/boosting 359 models, the optimizer preferred using class weighting ( class_weight = balanced ); random 360 forest settled on a moderate depth ( max_depth = 10) with 200 trees, and LightGBM retained 361
a compact conguration ( num_leaves = 31, learning_rate = 0.1, 100 estimators). 362 In contrast, the GRU required substantially more compute to tune (4118.1s), with the 363 selected setting using an embedding dimension ≈ 187, a large hidden size ≈ 734, a low 364 learning rate (4.5 × 10 − 4 ), and 8 epochs. This was ∼ 763 × slower than logistic regression, 365
∼ 189 × slower than SVM, and ∼ 88–144 × slower than the tree/boosting models, reecting 366
the higher search cost of neural architectures relative to classical methods. 367

When compute or turnaround 369 time is constrained, the linear, SVM, and tree/boosting families provide more favorable 370 tuning efciency than the GRU, while still allowing targeted adjustments (e.g., class weight- 371 ing for imbalanced data). All timings were obtained under the same environment; details 372
are provided in Methods. 373
3.2. Analysis of Model Performance 374 The results reveal two distinct patterns of model behavior, highlighting the critical 375
impact of class imbalance and the choice of loss function. 376
3.2.1. Performance Limitations of Classical Models 377 As shown in Table 2 , the four classical machine learning models (SVM, LR, RF, LGBM) 378 all appear to perform exceptionally well, with weighted precision, recall, and F1-scores at or 379 above 0.98. However, these metrics are highly misleading. Because the models were tuned 380 using the validation weighted F1-score ( f1_weighted ) as the hyperparameter selection 381 metric, a quantity dominated by the 98.9% majority (non-fraud) class, they learned to 382
achieve a high score by simply predicting "non-fraud" for nearly every case. 383
11 of 17 It is crucial to note that for Random Forest and LightGBM, the hyperparameter search 384 explicitly selected class_weight=‘balanced’ (see Table 1 ). Despite this mechanism— 385 which increases penalties for minority class errors—the models still converged on a high- 386 precision/low-recall solution. This underscores a critical nding: simply enabling a "bal- 387 anced" mode in standard libraries is often insufcient to overcome the inertia of the majority 388 class if the global validation metric (here, f1_weighted ) does not explicitly prioritize recall. 389

The Precision-Recall Trade-Off in the GRU Model 394 In stark contrast, the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) model, which was trained with a 395 class-weighted loss function, successfully learned to identify the minority class. This is 396 immediately visible in Table 2 , where its weighted recall (0.83) is much lower than the other 397
models, indicating it is not just predicting the majority class. 398 Table 3 shows the true result: the GRU model successfully identied 78% of all 399 fraudulent transactions (Recall = 0.78), a substantial improvement over the classical models. 400 Furthermore, its AUC of 0.8800 was the highest of all models, conrming its superior ability 401
to distinguish between the two classes. 402 However, this success in detection reveals the central challenge of this dataset. The 403 high recall was achieved at the cost of extremely low precision. With a Class 1 Precision 404 of 0.05 , the model generates approximately 19 false positives for every 1 true positive it 405 nds. This demonstrates a classic precision-recall trade-off, where the model is effective at 406
nding fraud but creates a signicant operational burden in doing so. 407

• False Alert Volume: At 5% precision, these 8,580 cases represent only 1/20th of the 415

• Stafng Implication: Assuming a fraud analyst can review 50 cases per day, this 419 model conguration would require approximately 13-14 full-time analysts working 420 for a full year (260 working days) just to clear the backlog for one million applications. 421 This calculation explicitly demonstrates the resource cost mentioned by the reviewers: high 422
recall comes with a substantial labor overhead. 423
3.4. Feature Importance Analysis 424 To understand the predictive logic of the models, we computed feature importances 425 for all ve architectures (Figures 1 through 5 ). For LR, RF, and LGBM, we used their native 426 model-based importances (coefcient magnitude or Gini/gain). For the non-linear SVM 427
and the GRU, we used permutation importance based on the drop in the F1-score. 428 The most signicant nding is the high degree of consensus across all models. Despite 429 their vastly different architectures and performance, all models identied the same core set 430 of features as the most predictive. The feature name_email_similarity was the undisputed 431 top predictor for all ve models, often by a signicant margin (see Figures 1 a, 2 a, etc.). To 432 clarify, this feature represents a normalized string distance metric (ranging from 0 to 1) 433 between the applicant’s provided name and their email user handle. A low score indicates 434 a mismatch (e.g., "John Doe" using "hacker123@email.com"), which is a primary indicator 435 of synthetic identity fraud where criminals use burner email addresses with stolen personal 436

nds to other top-tier features. The high importance of velocity_24h 438 and velocity_6h is similarly logical; these features track the count of applications asso- 439 ciated with the same device or IP address within a 6-hour or 24-hour sliding window. 440 High values are a proxy for automated "bot" attacks or "bust-out" fraud schemes where 441 criminals attempt to open multiple accounts in rapid succession. The income feature is 442 also a key differentiator, likely because fraudulent applications may use anomalously high 443 or low values that deviate from the patterns of legitimate applicants. The consistency of 444 these ndings provides strong evidence that all models, regardless of their success, are 445
identifying the correct, fundamental signals in the data. 446 This analysis provides a critical insight when combined with the performance results 447 from Section 3 . The performance gap of the classical models (LR, SVM, RF, LGBM) was 448 not a failure of feature identication; they correctly identied the same predictive features 449 as the successful GRU model. Their failure was one of objective. This is, in itself, an 450 important nding: the feature importance plots for the classical models effectively show us 451
the hallmarks of a non-fraudulent application. 452
Summary 453 Taken together with the performance analysis, these attributions indicate that the 454 classical models did not fail to discover informative signals; rather, tuning for f1_weighted 455 as the selection criterion under 1.10% prevalence biased them toward condent non- 456 fraud predictions, whereas the class-weighted GRU leveraged the same signals to recover 457
minority-class recall at the expected cost in precision. 458
4. Discussion 459 The empirical results of this study provide a clear and nuanced narrative regarding the 460 application of machine learning to a severely imbalanced fraud detection task. Our ndings 461 are discussed in three parts: an interpretation of the primary precision-recall trade-off, the 462
practical implications for real-world systems, and the limitations of this study. 463
4.1. Interpretation of Key Findings 464 The central nding of this paper is not simply that one model outperformed another, 465 but that the choice of optimization objective is profoundly more important than the choice 466
of model architecture . 467 The four classical models (SVM, LR, RF, LGBM) were not inherently "bad." On the 468 contrary, their high AUC scores (see Table 2 ) and their feature importance plots (Figures 2 - 4 ) 469 prove they were highly effective at one task: identifying the correct features. The feature 470 importance analysis shows a clear consensus: all models, including the GRU, agreed 471 that features like name_email_similarity and velocity_24h were the most predictive. 472 The failure of the classical models was one of objective. Tuned using f1_weighted as 473 the validation selection metric, a quantity dominated by the 98.9% majority class, the 474 models learned it was statistically "safer" to ignore the rare fraud signals and become 475 expert detectors of non-fraud . Their resulting 1-6% fraud recall is a direct and predictable 476 outcome of this-objective mismatch. This conrms the warnings found in earlier surveys 477 [ 10 ] regarding the dangers of accuracy-driven optimization, but extends those ndings by 478
quantifying exactly how much ’architecture’ matters when the objective is misaligned. 479 The GRU model, in contrast, was a statistical success precisely because its objective 480 (a class-weighted loss) was aligned with the problem. It was explicitly instructed to nd 481 the rare class, and it did, achieving a 78% recall. This conrms that the predictive signals 482 for fraud do exist in the data and that a deep learning architecture can effectively leverage 483
15 of 17 them. However, this statistical success immediately exposed the true challenge of this 484
domain: a severe precision-recall trade-off [ 19 ]. 485
4.2. Practical Implications: An Operational Bottleneck 486 The GRU model’s performance—78% recall at 5% precision—perfectly illustrates the 487 difference between a statistical solution and a practical one. While identifying 78% of fraud 488 is a signicant achievement, the 5% precision is operationally untenable in many business 489 contexts. This metric implies that for every 100 applications agged for manual review, 95 490 are false positives. This would overwhelm a human investigation team and likely be more 491
costly than the fraud it prevents. 492 This necessitates a shift from purely performance-based evaluation to economic cost 493 considerations, as demonstrated by Vanini et al. [ 12 ] . In their work, integrating economic 494 costs into the model selection process led to substantial loss reductions by optimizing for 495 low false-positive rates. Similarly, our ndings suggest that a bank cannot simply deploy 496 the "best AUC" model; they must determine an "optimal" threshold based on their specic 497
risk appetite and regulatory tolerance. 498 For instance, a regulated institution facing heavy nes for money laundering (AML) 499 violations might tolerate the high operational cost of the 5% precision model to ensure 500 maximum recall. Conversely, a ntech focused on frictionless user experience might 501 prefer a stricter threshold to reduce customer friction. In a hypothetical scenario used 502 for illustration, such an institution might accept a lower recall of 50% in exchange for a 503 precision of 20%. This alignment of model thresholds with institutional strategy resonates 504 with broader nance research on risk behavior, where the salience of specic risks drives 505 decision-making [ 26 ]. Ultimately, the "right" model is not dened by the F1-score, but by 506
the institution’s capacity to absorb the cost of intervention versus the cost of fraud losses. 507 The practical value of this GRU model, therefore, is not as a nal decision-maker. 508 Instead, it should be viewed as an exceptionally effective triage and ltering tool . It 509 successfully reduced the problem from 1 million "unknown" applications to a much smaller, 510 high-risk pool, which can then be fed into a more specialized (or costly) second-stage 511 analysis. This suggests a hybrid approach, where the high-recall/low-precision model 512 serves as the rst-pass lter for a system designed to manage, rather than eliminate, the 513
operational cost of false positives. 514
4.3. Limitations and Future Work 515 This study’s ndings, while clear, are bounded by several methodological choices that 516
open avenues for future research. 517
1. Choice of Imbalance Technique: We focused exclusively on one technique: class- 518 weighted loss. This is a powerful method, but it is not the only one. Future work 519 should compare our GRU’s performance against other strategies, such as algorithm- 520 level approaches (e.g., Focal Loss [ 8 ]) or data-level approaches (e.g., SMOTE oversam- 521
pling or under-sampling the majority class). 522
2. Deep Learning Architectures: The GRU, a recurrent model, was used to process 523 tabular data as a sequence. While effective, it is not a traditional architecture for 524 this data type. A valuable next step would be to benchmark this model against 525 transformers designed specically for tabular data, such as a TabTransformer, to see if 526
attention-based mechanisms can better model the feature interactions. 527
3. Generalizability and Fraud Prevalence: Our analysis relies on the BAF dataset with 528 a xed 1.1% fraud prevalence. While this is representative of many onboarding 529 scenarios, ndings may differ in domains with moderately higher prevalence (e.g., 530 credit card fraud at 5-10%) or different feature distributions. Future studies should 531
16 of 17 simulate varying prevalence rates (e.g., by subsampling negatives) to determine the 532
"break-even" point where classical models might recover performance. 533
4. Alternative Strategies (Ensembles): We treated models as competitors, but in practice, 534 they can be collaborators. A promising avenue for future work is to explore ensemble 535 or two-stage architectures . For example, the high-recall GRU could serve as a "nomi- 536 nator" to ag potential fraud, while a high-precision Random Forest could serve as 537 a "validator" to lter out false positives. Such hybrid approaches could potentially 538
optimize the precision-recall trade-off better than any single model. 539
5. Threshold Tuning: Our results report metrics at the default 0.5 classication thresh- 540 old. Given the severe precision-recall trade-off, this is not the optimal threshold for 541 deployment. A critical next step, which we recommend for any practical application, 542 is to analyze the full Precision-Recall Curve (which is more informative than the ROC 543 curve in imbalanced settings [ 9 , 20 ]). By "moving the threshold," an organization could 544 select a different operating point, for example, hypothetically accepting a lower recall 545
of 50% in exchange for a more manageable precision of 20%. 546
6. Analysis of False Positives: The 5% precision of the GRU model is not merely a 547 performance decit; it is a source of data. A qualitative analysis of the false positives— 548 the legitimate cases that "look" fraudulent to the model—could reveal new insights, 549
identify feature engineering opportunities, or highlight biases in the dataset [ 27 ]. 550
4.4. Concluding Remarks 551 Taken together, our results show that in extremely imbalanced onboarding settings the 552 decisive levers are what we optimize and where we operate , rather than model family per se. 553 On the BAF benchmark, standard f1_weighted selection produced classical baselines with 554 supercially strong aggregate scores yet negligible fraud recall, whereas a class-weighted 555 GRU recovered minority detection (78% recall) at the expected cost in precision (5%). For 556 practice, this reframes fraud modeling as a joint objective–threshold design problem: align 557 the training objective with minority-class capture and set the operating point to the review 558 budget and risk tolerance. For research, it motivates reporting precision–recall behavior and 559 simple workload proxies (e.g., FPs per TP) alongside aggregate metrics to make operational 560 trade-offs explicit. This clarity—of objective, operating point, and reporting—provides a 561
principled path from statistical performance to deployable value. 562
